<STRUCT_0001>
Let <MATH_0001> be a presentation of an algebraic stack.
Then the properties of the diagonal of <MATH_0002> over <MATH_0003>, are
the properties of the morphism <MATH_0004>. For example,
if <MATH_0005> for some smooth group <MATH_0006> in algebraic spaces
over <MATH_0007> then <MATH_0008> is the structure morphism <MATH_0009>. Hence the diagonal
is not automatically separated itself (contrary to what happens in the
case of schemes and algebraic spaces). To say that <MATH_0010> is quasi-separated
over <MATH_0011> should certainly imply that <MATH_0012> is quasi-compact, but we
hesitate to say that <MATH_0013> is quasi-separated over <MATH_0014> without also
requiring the morphism <MATH_0015> to be quasi-separated. In other words,
requiring the diagonal morphism to be quasi-compact does not really agree
with our intuition for a ``quasi-separated algebraic stack'', and we should
also require the diagonal itself to be quasi-separated.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
What about ``separated algebraic stacks''? We have seen in
Morphisms of Spaces,
Lemma <REF_0001>
that an algebraic space is separated if and only if the diagonal is proper.
This is the condition that is usually used to define separated algebraic
stacks too. In the example <MATH_0016> above this means that <MATH_0017>
is a proper group scheme. This means algebraic stacks of the form
<MATH_0018> are proper over <MATH_0019> where <MATH_0020> is an elliptic curve
over <MATH_0021> (insert future reference here). In certain situations it may be
more natural to assume the diagonal is finite.
